title: CHAPTER EIGHT. On God's absolute necessity of existing; definition
english: CHAPTER EIGHT. On God's absolute necessity of existing.

Thus far concerning the attributes of God which stand in place of properties consequent upon His essence in general: now, about to speak of the several ones separately and distinctly, there occurs before the rest I. Absolute necessity of existing, which is that perfection of God by which He so is or exists that He cannot not be.

The sacred letters point out this attribute by the names of immortality and incorruptibility (1 Timothy 6:16-17; Romans 1:23). It is called a perfection of God for the foundation of that negation by which we declare this necessity, which is a positive perfection that truly exists in God, which materially, as they commonly speak, is signified by this attribute. But its formal ratio is placed in the negation of some imperfection which commonly inheres in all creatures and is called contingency.

title: Necessity distinguished from immutability and eternity
english: But he errs who thinks this attribute ought to be reduced either to immutability or to eternity. For just as for things to be changed properly is not for them either to be produced so that they are, or to be destroyed so that they are not, but with existence remaining safe to acquire or lose something formally — so conversely to be immutable is not the same as not to be able not to be; but properly signifies not to be able to acquire a new perfection, or to be deprived of any, with existence remaining safe.

From which it is gathered that necessity of existing and immutability differ not a little; since this is opposed to mutability, that to contingency. But eternity is nearer to this necessity, although they differ in this, that this denies the beginning and end of duration, but that denies contingency or the power of not existing: and therefore, as immutability is a certain [cause] of eternity, of which it is the prior cause and reason, so this necessity [is a cause] of eternity. And so we conclude that God is eternal — that is, lacks beginning and end of His duration — from this, that He Himself is a necessary being, to whom not to be is altogether adverse.

title: Proper to God alone; created 'necessaries' only secundum quid
english: But we assert that this absolute necessity of existing is so proper to God that it can be attributed to no creature. For created 'necessaries' only in a certain respect

title: Demonstration: Scripture, the Name, reason from independence
english: But we demonstrate that God is an absolutely necessary being, FIRST, by the testimonies of sacred Scripture (1 Timothy 6:16-17; Romans 1:23; Psalm 102:27-28), where God is called immortal and incorruptible and is opposed to corruptible things, and is established always to remain, to declare absolute necessity of existing. From which also Augustine (On the Trinity 1.1): Although, he says, the soul is said to be immortal in a manner, the Apostle would not say, Who alone has immortality, unless because true immortality is incommutability, which no creature can have, since it belongs to the Creator alone.

SECOND, by the Name of God, Eheje (Exodus 3:14), by which absolute necessity of existing is indicated, as Nazianzen (Oration 24 / 2 on theology) and Augustine (On True Religion, chapter 49) testify. For this reason God also attributes Being to Himself alone, as He who alone is necessarily (Isaiah 42:8; Amos 5:8).

THIRD, by reason. For every independent being, and what exists from itself, is absolutely necessary. God is an independent being, existing namely from Himself, as was demonstrated in chapter 2 on God's existence. Therefore God is an absolutely necessary being.

title: Major proved; pagan confession — Cap. 8 close
english: The major is proved in two ways. First, because an independent being or one existing from itself exists by the force of its essence or nature, and therefore existence belongs to it as necessarily as essence. Second, because an independent being neither could once not have been, nor hereafter not be. Therefore it is absolutely necessary.

FOURTH, also by the confession of Gentile philosophers. For Orpheus spoke of the necessity of all things — that is, a substance which is necessarily through itself, and on which all the rest depend, but itself on none. Aristotle calls God a necessary, perpetual being. Apuleius: I would judge necessity itself to be called nothing other than God. Avicenna: That holy thing is the necessary being which is from itself, but not the remaining beings, even if they have necessity of existing from another.
